reports.title: State of Cognitive Bias Evidence 2026
reports.summary: A data-backed review of where common cognitive-bias claims look strong, mixed, easy to confuse, or still under-reviewed.

sections.heading: Corrections usually help more than the backfire story suggests
sections.interpretation: Backfire is a memorable claim, but the reviewed evidence does not support treating it as the normal result of correction. The useful distinction is between disagreement, incomplete updating and a measured increase in the false belief.

sections.heading: Retrospective judgment needs two different checks
sections.interpretation: Knowing the outcome can distort both perceived predictability and evaluation of the earlier decision. Keeping forecasts and decision rationales before the outcome gives reviewers something better than reconstructed memory.

sections.heading: Repetition is not independent evidence
sections.interpretation: Repeated claims can feel more true even when repetition adds no new evidence. This matters especially when several pages or AI outputs are recycling the same source.

sections.heading: Uncertainty is a result, not a publishing failure
sections.interpretation: Mixed, contested and unreviewed states are useful outputs. They show where a confident internet summary would be stronger than the reviewed evidence.

reports.uncertainty: This report summarizes the reviewed subset of the Cognitive Biases corpus. It is not a systematic review of every cognitive-bias study, and coverage is uneven across concepts.
